column2: I don’t feel safe because aside from a couple miles on Erie Blvd, we don’t have truly protected bike lanes. I commute on the Genesee St. bike lane but it’s definitely more of a suggestion than a designated area for bikers to safely commute. Cars swerve into the bike lane, open car doors into it, park in it, etc. And having a suggested bike lane like the one on Genesee is best case scenario for Syracuse — most other streets have nothing to even signal to cars that a biker might be riding on the same road. When I think about where I want to buy a house in the city, I do take into consideration how safely I’ll be able to commute. For example, I like Tipp Hill and Strathmore neighborhoods but it’s a nightmare biking to/from because of how unsafe the roads are — so I won’t consider buying a house in those neighborhoods. column2:
I am a very experienced and aggressive rider. 
It took me years to realize this. 

I find that it is important to make eye contact with motorists; and a friend long ago taught me that looking at the tires/rims of a car for motion is a better indicator than looking at the entire vehicle itself. While I am likely a nuisance to motorists sometimes, I find it important to make eye contact - for my safety and to transmit acknowledgement through a sincere polite nod or wave, to help register to them that you are human. It's important to be kind and rise above the car v. cyclist stigma, so that the motorist mindset might have hope of changing - one interaction at a time.. there are too many cyclists that act with animosity toward motorists, and it only breeds resentment and compounds negative attitudes. I also feel / have heard from research, that it is important to ride in plain clothes to look as much like a human as possible (sans spandex, sans helmet) to further remind motorists that we are people. I suppose I'm implying the opposite is true too.. remembering motorists are people too.. even if they seem like awful automatons that are slowly dying inside from an unsustainable lifestyle that leads to systematic reliance on increasing financial obligation and contributing to their own expense, wasted time, and poor health... instead of the freedom of bipedal transportation.
column3:
More dedicated/separated bike lanes are important for new cyclists to feel safe riding their bikes. 

We (Syracuse) are far behind the curve in bicycle culture.. and there seems to be a pervasive belief that bikes are for children, sport, and/or the wealthy. This is an infuriating and inconvenient mindset.. especially because the entitlement is held so strong with motorists, despite that we all must share the roads, and we all support the associated costs, yet the high cost of upkeep is demanded for the benefit of motor vehicles.. (so as much as I'd prefer to just be visible and take a lane and save $$ for municipalities.. it is important to build awareness and cycling culture through safe infrastructure) 

it's possible that some sort of education campaign could work.. but doubtful.. "more people on bikes" is a thing people say, and that seems to be the only way.. and to do that, it needs to be made easier
column4: indifferent for myself. frustrating that the culture is lagging behind... so I suppose I feel a tug to be somewhere where it isn't so strange or difficult to ride a bike instead or using a car as the norm

column2:
Car drivers are generally nice but a few aggressive ones are enough to make me afraid. They drive up too close, or honk at me for no clear reason, which startle me and I often can't react in time to find out who's honking and why and if I need to get out of the way. A lot of drivers just seem really poorly educated and yell at me to get on the sidewalk. If I do that I get yelled at by pedestrians. It's a no win.

When it snows, the ploughs push all the snow to the sides where I ride. If I take the lane I get cursed at, yelled at, or honked at, or get aggressively taken over. The bike lanes also often don't get ploughed in time and are super packed with ice. 

The constant construction is also a problem. Construction vehicles often park in bike lanes or obstruct them or have dangerous debris.
